author: Mithun Roy
text:
A few weeks of evenings went into this one. FinLens reads a financial document and answers questions about it without making up the numbers.

Drop in an invoice or a card statement and ask something like “why was this charge so high?” It finds the answer in the document and the policy behind it, and every figure links back to the exact spot on the page it came from.

The retrieval was the easy part. Stopping the model from inventing numbers was not.

A few things that worked:

The numbers never come from the LLM. Line items and totals are read straight from the PDF’s table structure. The model handles wording, but if it tries to state an amount, that amount has to appear word-for-word in the document or it gets rejected. It can read. It can’t invent.

I chunk one table row at a time and never split a row. Split a row and the description ends up stuck to the wrong number, which was the single biggest source of wrong answers I ran into.

Grounding is checked, not trusted. Citations get matched against the chunks that were actually retrieved, and any number that can’t be traced to a source is flagged before you see it.

Ask it something the documents don’t cover and it tells you it can’t answer instead of guessing.

Built with Python, LangChain, ChromaDB, Groq running Llama 3.3 70B, MiniLM embeddings, a Next.js frontend on Vercel, and a FastAPI backend on Render. Everything runs on free tiers. I never put in a card.

author: Nermeen Nasim
text:
I keep seeing "AI engineer," "ML engineer," and "prompt engineer" used like they're the same role. In practice, I've found they solve pretty different problems — here's how I've come to think about the split.

𝗠𝗟 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴
Starts from data. You train or fine-tune a model from scratch, and the product gets built once the model is good enough. The core skill is modeling itself.

𝗔𝗜 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴
Starts from a foundation model someone else already trained — GPT, Claude, Llama. The work shifts to adapting it: prompting, retrieval, context construction, fine-tuning when it's actually needed, plus the evaluation and infrastructure that keeps it reliable once real users touch it.


The part I think matters most, for devs and non-devs alike: the build order flips.
 Classic ML engineering goes data → model → product. 

AI engineering tends to go product → data → model — you can ship something useful on an existing model almost right away, then invest in data and fine-tuning once it proves out. That's a big reason full-stack backgrounds translate so well here.


And prompt engineering fits inside that second one, not next to it. Writing a good prompt is one piece of the adaptation work — alongside retrieval, evaluation, and interface design. Useful skill, just a narrower slice than "AI engineering" as a whole.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝗻
Agents add a layer on top of this, not a separate category. An agentic app isn't one prompt in, one answer out — it's a model that can plan, call tools, check its own work, and take several steps toward a goal. Still the same AI engineering foundations (context, evaluation, infrastructure); they're just applied to a system that acts, not just responds.

The harder question isn't "agent or not," it's how much you let it decide on its own. Most teams I've seen land somewhere on a spectrum: heavy human-in-the-loop while the system is new and every output gets reviewed, then the AI handling lower-stakes internal steps once it's earned some trust, and only later, if ever, acting autonomously on anything customer-facing or high-stakes. Jumping straight to "fully autonomous" before the accuracy backs it up is usually where things break.


If you're not building this day to day, the practical version: "can write good prompts" and "can adapt and productionize a model reliably" are different bars when you're hiring or scoping AI work. And when someone pitches you an "AI agent," it's worth asking where it sits on that spectrum — suggesting, acting internally, or acting on its own toward customers.


Genuinely curious how others draw these lines, especially anyone who's hired for these roles, built agentic workflows, or had to decide how much autonomy to hand an AI system. Where does this match your experience, and where does it break down?

author: Luke Butler
text:
Everyone wants to hire AI talent right now, but almost no one knows how to assess it.  

I'm seeing organisations post for AI Engineers when they mean Data Analysts. 

I'm seeing others ask for Machine Learning Engineers when they mean "someone to use an off-the-shelf API". 

Others hire people with impressive GitHub portfolios but who've never deployed anything into a regulated environment.  

The AI talent market is moving faster than hiring processes, which means the gap between what you think you're getting and what you're actually getting can be enormous.  

Before you write a job brief, you need to answer three questions: 
1️⃣ Are we building or integrating? 
2️⃣ What does "production" actually mean for this role?
3️⃣ Who will this person work with and what do those people need from them? 

Start there, then call me, and everything else will fall in to place.

text:
From a small town to earning a Master’s in Data Science in the UK - a dream that once felt impossible is now a reality. 🎓🇬🇧

I am proud to share that I have graduated with a Master’s in Data Science from Aston University, Birmingham.

This achievement means far more than earning a degree.

I lost both my parents when I was 12. Since then, my uncle has been my greatest source of strength. He made countless sacrifices and always encouraged me to continue my education. Coming from a humble background, studying abroad once seemed impossible.

Today, I stand as a graduate because of his unwavering belief in me. This milestone belongs to him as much as it belongs to me.

During my Master’s, I completed a research project titled “Explainable AI for Predicting Pneumonia Using Chest X-Ray Images.” The project explored how Explainable AI can improve transparency and trust in medical image classification. I am grateful that this work also led to a published research paper.

Alongside my degree, I completed:

* Data Analysis and Visualization with Microsoft Power BI - Microsoft & Coursera
* Introduction to Data Science in Python - University of Michigan & Coursera

These experiences strengthened my skills in data analytics, visualisation, machine learning, Python, Power BI, and Explainable AI.

My heartfelt thanks go to Matthew Bickley, my personal tutor at Aston University, for his guidance and encouragement throughout this journey.

I am also grateful to Square Associates Pte Ltd, Singapore, for giving me an internship opportunity where I gained valuable industry exposure and practical experience.

I used OpenAI’s ChatGPT responsibly as a learning assistant to understand concepts, explore solutions, troubleshoot challenges, and improve my technical knowledge.

Most importantly, thank you to my uncle, family, friends, lecturers, and mentors. Your support made this achievement possible.

Graduation is not the end—it is the beginning of a new chapter. 🚀

I am currently seeking graduate and entry-level opportunities in:

* Data Science and Data Analytics

* Business Intelligence and Power BI
* Python Development

I am eager to apply my skills, research experience, and passion for solving real-world problems. If your organisation is hiring or you can refer me to a suitable opportunity, I would be grateful to hear from you.

Here’s to new beginnings, continuous growth, and lifelong learning! 🌟

Here's how to use your prep content to stand out and win the offer.

Interviewers instantly recognize mastery when you use precise PM language. Sprinkle terms like:

value delivery
predictive vs. adaptive approaches
risk escalation paths
servant leadership

This signals that you think and communicate like a project leader.



2. Turn exam scenarios into interview stories

Every PMP practice question is a workplace scenario. Convert them into STAR‑format stories:

Conflict resolution
Stakeholder alignment
Risk mitigation
Team leadership

author: Hassan Jameh
text:
They have a signal problem.

There are 6.9 million open roles in the U.S. and the hires rate is sitting at 3.1%, the lowest since April 2020.

That gap says a lot.

Plenty of jobs.

Plenty of applicants.

Still slow hiring.

I see the same pattern in IT environments.

A ticket queue can be full and still have the wrong work at the top.

A recruiter queue works the same way.

Applications come in.

Most of them need sorting, checking, follow-up, context, salary alignment, language fit, location fit, timing fit, manager fit.

Then the hiring manager says: “Can we see more profiles?”

That sentence is expensive.

Average time-to-fill is now 44 days.

For technical roles, time to first fill is around 10 weeks.

That’s a long time when the team is already missing someone who can run endpoint rollouts, clean up identity issues, support researchers, or keep an Agile delivery moving.

The structural issue is simple:

🔸 Job boards create volume  
They account for 49% of applications, but only 24.6% of hires. More inbound doesn’t automatically mean more useful matches.

🔸 Recruiters carry too many open roles  
The average is 14 open requisitions per recruiter. That changes the job from judgment to triage.

🔸 AI saves time, but it doesn’t fix bad input  
43% of organizations use AI in HR. 89% of HR users say it saves time. Only 17% call the implementation highly successful. That tells me the tool is helping with speed, but the process around it is still weak.

Recruiting works best when the role is explained like an operational problem.

What breaks if this person is missing?

What systems will they touch?

Who will they support?

What does good look like after the first quarter?

I learned this teaching ICT to newly arrived immigrants in Sweden.

Same classroom.

Different languages.

Different starting points.

The work was finding the shortest path between where someone was and where they needed to be.

Recruiters do that too.

The good ones don’t just “find candidates.”

They translate messy business needs into a person who can actually do the work.

If you want faster hiring, start by giving recruiters a cleaner problem.

What would change in your hiring process if every role started with the real operational gap, not the job description?

text:
AI GOVERNANCE JUST BECAME AN OPERATING REQUIREMENT.

August 2 marks a meaningful AI Act milestone in Europe: transparency rules begin to apply. People must be informed when they are interacting with AI, and certain AI-generated content — including deepfakes and public-interest material — must be identifiable. This is not just a legal update for software companies. It is a signal that AI is moving from experimentation into the operating model of every business that touches customers, employees, or the public.

The strategic mistake is treating compliance as a document you finish at the end. The businesses that handle this well will build transparency into the workflow itself: label the chatbot, log the decision path, define who reviews high-impact outputs, and know which tools are creating or changing customer-facing content. Governance becomes infrastructure — as ordinary and necessary as access controls, backups, and financial approvals.

This matters even if you are not based in the EU. Digital products, global teams, vendors, and customer relationships cross borders. More importantly, the EU is setting a direction other markets are likely to study: trust will increasingly be part of the product experience. A company that can explain where AI is used, what it can do, and where a human remains accountable will earn more confidence than one that simply says it is powered by AI.

For business owners, map your AI use, classify the risk, document the human handoff, and make disclosure part of the customer journey. Start with the boring systems — intake, support, recruiting, marketing content, and approvals. Boring is where the money is, and it is also where a clear operating standard protects you.

The winners will not necessarily have the most AI. They will have the clearest rules for using it well. Is your business treating AI governance as paperwork — or as a competitive advantage?

Maybe I hold my hope for Humanity a bit too high: Still, I can't wrap my head around How is this possible these convos, and easily deflatable misconceptions still find resonances, polute spaces and waste everybody's time in 2026: 

"AI did this!!"

No, either someone human LETS this happen through poor Agency, weak AQE testing, Deterministic Software bias, or several dozen uncharted skills or process blueprint alignements. || OR, - if can't make sense of the behavior - The outcome/output is the PLAN.     

"Work Removed? Work HAS moved"

A report that once required three hours may now arrive as a convincing draft in three minutes.
The recovered time goes into checking facts, spotting the missing assumption, removing elegant nonsense and deciding whether the document deserves to exist.
• Poor adoption produces more emails, decks and synthetic activity. Mature adoption creates room to question the brief and stop weak decisions before they become expensive.
The blank page occupies less of the day. Judgement carries more weight. A respectable first version becomes common; recognising what should survive it remains scarce.

"The Paretto blindness epidemic"

Companies assume that broad access will create broadly similar gains.
Corporate methods are ageing faster than training systems can replace them. Consulting loses part of its gatekeeping role. Product teams no longer hold a monopoly on weak signals.

That instability encourages a daily dose of relativism:
“If God is dead — RIP the pacing of continuous training, the consulting monopoly on specialised knowledge and the old rituals of product development — is everything permitted?”
The standards remain, but they are less procedural, harder to certify and concentrated in fewer people.
• Problem selection, probabilistic thinking, Bayesian updates, agency, discernement, intellectual range and taste.
How would a company teach a Renaissance mindset at scale? Agency to someone whose survival has depended on permission? Taste, beyond examples of what looked good last quarter?
Frameworks and mentorship help. These qualities grow through curiosity, exposure, consequences and repeated correction. A two-hour webinar cannot distribute them evenly.

Pareto blindness begins when organisations expect the gains to spread aproximately evenly because everyone has access.
A smaller group may become several times more effective. Others may produce more acceptable material with greater independant speed.
An organisation can report widespread adoption while relying on the few able to turn the technology into sound judgement.

Are we still recruiting for reliable task execution while the environment has started selecting for learning velocity, agency and taste?

The asteroid is visible. Misnaming it will not alter its trajectory.

text:
“Agile doesn’t work”. We’ve heard it. It’s time to reimagine it.

Last week, I participated in the PMI Agile Alliance Reimagining Agility Workshop at the Gaylord National Harbor, Maryland. Reimagining Agility is an initiative to:

1.     Expand Agile values and principles beyond the IT team to include broader enterprise functions and business strategy. 

2.     Address how AI is shifting team structures, automating tasks, and necessitating human judgement.

3.     Focus on delivering value over ritualized mechanics and processes.

Our team’s wicked problem focused on roles, responsibilities, and organizational structure.  

The Problem: 
Agile roles are ambiguous and confusing both in and out of the IT team, organization, community, and industry. For example, one company may simply rename all project managers to scrum masters, while another company may name all scrum masters “collaboration evangelists” to avoid the term “master”.  

For the Agile practitioner, this creates difficulty defining and demonstrating transferable skills and competencies on their resume and LinkedIn profile when seeking their next assignment. For organizations, this creates difficulty in recruiting and filling roles effectively and efficiently when HR doesn’t understand Agile nor the roles.

The result is a mismatch between skills and needs on the team, causing delays and misunderstandings in the work to be delivered. And so… “Agile doesn’t work.”

The Solution:
A matrix of clear, simple, and generic Agile roles based on skills, capabilities, and value delivered in conjunction with a career ladder illustrating expertise gained over time. A generic Agile org chart illustrates how the roles interact on the team and within the enterprise to enable scaling.

The future is here. Let’s make Agile work for the next 25 years!

What is the impact of #AI in our roles? 

Over the past couple of months, I’ve attended recruiting events and technical workshops across colleges, high schools, and organizations like #Microsoft and #BCIT, on behalf of my organization #BCHydro. One question kept coming up from junior analysts, data scientists, and early‑career product professionals: “Is AI going to replace our roles, and how do I make sure I’m not replaceable?”

As someone who manages programs across data, analytics, and product‑driven tech stacks, here’s my honest answer: AI is transforming our work, but it is not replacing you.

AI can accelerate your work by summarizing trends, generating hypotheses, automating repetitive analysis, and speeding up exploration.

But AI cannot:

• Understand customers
• Navigate ambiguity
• Influence stakeholders
• Validate its own outcome 
• Coach and mentor junior professionals
• Defend the business in important meetings when metrics are challenged


This is why analytics‑oriented people remain essential. Your value isn’t in producing dashboards; it’s in ensuring insights are real, meaningful, and actionable based on your business knowledge. That’s the skillset not everyone has.

If you’re early in your career, invest in skills AI amplifies rather than replaces:

• Business acumen
• Decision science
• Critical interpretation

Many of the most successful technical program and product managers I’ve worked with are analytics oriented. Those foundations made them exceptional leaders in today’s AI‑enabled environment.

Whether you’re early in your career or a senior leader mentoring teams, I’d love to hear your perspective. How do you see AI reshaping analytics, data science, and product management?

Amazon 60 Minutes for each candidate and she was handeling 20 and more positions ? It jsut takes 10 to 15 min to realize a person is perfect candidate or not !!! An now we are victims of their personal tools !! This is insane !!!This is an interesting initiative, but as an infrastructure project manager with more than 15 years of experience working directly with heads of engineering, technical teams, recruiting departments, and HR, I believe it raises several important governance questions.
Over the past decade, I have applied for several Amazon infrastructure and program-management positions. Only one Amazon recruiter contacted me, for a position in Texas that I could not accept because of the location. That experience makes me wonder how many qualified candidates with transferable technical and leadership experience are filtered out before an engineering leader or hiring manager ever reviews them.
Supporting more than 20 open positions is a significant workload. Sixty minutes of research may create a useful starting point, but technical roles across cloud, networking, data centers, security, software, AI, and infrastructure require careful calibration with engineering SMEs. A marketing-management background is not inherently disqualifying for recruiting, but it cannot replace deep technical validation when defining target profiles or interpreting transferable experience.
Could Amazon clarify:
• Was this PartyRock application reviewed and approved by PXT, Legal, Privacy, Information Security, and Responsible AI teams?
• What “historical team information,” internal reporting, or other company data is entered into the application?
• Is the tool limited to sourcing research, or is it also used to scan, score, rank, include, or exclude candidates?
• How are accuracy, bias, explainability, data retention, security, and auditability evaluated?
• Do engineering leaders and technical hiring managers validate the profiles and transferable skills generated by the tool?
• Are candidates informed when AI meaningfully influences sourcing or initial screening?
Returning 115 hours to the business is valuable, but efficiency should be measured alongside hiring quality, fairness, candidate access, and the number of qualified people who might otherwise be overlooked.
The strongest model is not AI replacing technical judgment. It is AI-assisted, technically calibrated, transparent, and human-accountable recruiting.
